title: Circular Cities: Fix It, Reuse It, Don't Trash It
summary:
Suppose a seam splits on your shoe, or a favorite toy breaks. Do you throw it away — or fix it? Now imagine a whole city asking that question about almost everything.

That is the idea behind circular cities. Some 100 communities around the world are trying to keep materials in use for as long as possible, looping them into repairs, reuse, and recycling instead of sending them to the trash.

Most products today follow a straight line: companies gather raw materials, factories build products, people use them until they break or go out of style, and then they are thrown away. Only a very small fraction get recycled. Circular cities aim for a closed loop instead. When something can be used again, it is. When there is waste, it is recycled, and recovered materials cut the cost and resources needed to make new things.

Landfills are part of the problem. They are filling up, and most release methane, a greenhouse gas that drives climate change. Some also leak metals and toxic chemicals. Making replacement products creates still more pollution.

Austin, Texas, shows what a city can do. Its Resource Recovery department runs a yearly toy-repair clinic, fix-it workshops, and online videos to help people keep valued things out of the trash. Fifteen years ago, Austin set a goal of diverting 90 percent of its waste from landfills by 2040.

Amsterdam in the Netherlands hopes to have almost no waste by 2050. There, one clever project reuses rainwater under artificial grass fields: a layer beneath the turf catches the water, which later wicks upward and evaporates, cooling the surface for players and easing the load on the city's storm-water system.

City governments are also big buyers, which gives them power to push companies toward greener goods. Sacha Stolp, who heads innovation in Amsterdam's Future-Proof Assets Program, says that as big buyers, cities can ask companies for more valuable solutions. The message is simple: just because something is broken does not mean its use has to stop.
why_it_matters: Throwaway habits fill landfills and drive pollution, so keeping things in use longer protects the climate and saves the materials needed to make replacements.

A circular city tries to break that pattern by keeping products and materials in use through repair, reuse, and recycling.
Repair clinics and fix-it workshops help people mend broken things instead of replacing them.
When cities buy goods in large amounts, they can also push companies to make products that last longer and are easier to reuse.
